definition: Learning a mapping from inputs to outputs from labeled examples, such as (image, object class) pairs.
details: In supervised learning the training data carries ground-truth labels, and the model is scored against them during training. It covers classification and regression and is the most common paradigm, but it depends on the availability and quality of labeled data.

explainer.lead: Supervised learning is the dominant way models are trained, and its performance ceiling is set by the labels it learns from. It matters because nearly every deployed classifier or predictor depends on it, and label quality often matters more than model choice.

tiers.eli5: It's like learning with an answer key: you see many problems with the correct answers written down, and you learn the rule that turns one into the other.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers fit the model on labeled training pairs and score it against ground-truth labels during training. The common pitfall is assuming more data helps when the labels themselves are noisy or inconsistent.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, learning a mapping f from inputs X to outputs Y from labeled pairs, covering classification and regression. Its main known limit is dependence on the availability and quality of labeled data.

explainer.example: Training an object detector on (image, object class) pairs, where each image's ground-truth class labels are used to score the model during training.
